Interior design brief template

A useful brief turns discovery into a small set of decisions that the project can return to. It says what the room needs to do, what cannot change, and which questions still need an answer.

By OpenLintel · Updated September 26, 2026 · Educational resource

Worked example & fields

Illustrative teaching extension of The Window Room. Pending review; not a client record, supplier quote, site survey, or construction-ready document.

Worked example preview · DOCX

Project purpose

Describe the change the project should achieve in one sentence, without naming products too early.

A place to read. A place to gather. A little more room for everyday life.

Room and source information

Record the room reference, dimension source, survey date, and confidence. Nominal dimensions are not site verification.

The Window Room: 5000 × 4000 mm; ceiling 2800 mm. Nominal sample dimensions, not a survey.

Functional priorities

Rank activities and distinguish essential needs from optional additions.

Bring reading, conversation, and storage into one room.

Retained conditions

State fixed conditions and what requires condition checks.

Retain the existing oak floor; Keep the window and entrance positions; Bring reading, conversation, and storage into one room

Design direction

Name the agreed concept and explain why it serves the brief. Keep alternatives identifiable.

Pale oak, warm mineral walls, and linen. A calm material palette lets the light and the existing floor lead.

Deliverables and exclusions

List the proposed outputs; refer to a separate scope document for responsibility and limits.

Illustrative brief, concept comparison, WR-01 furnished plan, WR-02 joinery elevation, and partial materials schedule. No construction-ready package.

Open decisions

Record the question, required information, owner, and next review. Unknown is a valid status.

Wall finish area to survey; final sofa model and supplier to specify; budget and dates not established.

Review record

Capture the revision, reviewer, date, and what was agreed. A filled example is not actual approval.

R0; pending review; no client approval represented.

How to use this template

Complete this after discovery, not instead of discovery. Read the objectives back to the client in plain language. Revisit the brief when scope changes rather than quietly changing its meaning in a presentation. Preserve the agreed brief revision when discussing new needs; review effects on scope separately.

  1. Extract needs and constraints from the questionnaire.
  2. Check each proposed deliverable against the objectives.
  3. Confirm unresolved items and review the brief before starting the next phase.

Make the brief testable without specifying too early

A brief should help you compare options against the same requirements. Separate a need, a retained condition, and a proposed response. If the response changes, the underlying need may remain valid.

A later request for another room is not a minor wording edit. Record it as a possible scope change and review its effects before inserting it into the agreed baseline.

Review before use

  • Avoid vague aims such as “make it better” without explaining use.
  • Do not hide exclusions in notes that nobody reviews.
  • Do not treat a signed-off aesthetic direction as approval of dimensions or cost.

Units, source information, and US use

The worked example keeps its original nominal metric dimensions. For a US project, choose and label a primary imperial or metric convention, distinguish item counts from areas, and document any display conversion and rounding. Never relabel metric values as imperial or treat conversion as site verification.

Make it your own

Separate blank and worked-example documents. Edit the blank copy in Word or a compatible document editor. Any PDF is a printable companion, not an interactive form.
